opus-5.5.text:
I think it's sooner than a lot of people expect, though I'd frame it carefully, because "real-world use" doesn't have to mean a fully general home robot that does everything. What matters for the flywheel is getting robots deployed doing *something* useful, in a setting where they gather experience and get better at it.

If I had to put a number on it, I'd say single-digit years. Something like one to two years for real deployments in narrower settings, and maybe around five years for a much more general system that can do a wide range of household tasks. I hold those numbers loosely. In this field the hard part is often not where you expect it to be.

The reason I'm fairly optimistic is that the ingredients are coming together. Over the last couple of years we've seen that robotic foundation models, trained on large and diverse datasets and built on top of vision-language models, really do generalize. They can fold laundry they haven't seen before, clean up kitchens they haven't been in, and follow language instructions. They're not perfect, but they're competent enough to be useful in some settings, and that's the threshold you need. You don't need a robot that's perfect on day one. You need one that's good enough to be worth deploying, so it can start collecting the data that makes it better.

That's what makes the flywheel so important. With language models, the internet already existed, so you had this huge reservoir of data before you even started. Robotics doesn't have that. The data has to come from robots doing things in the world. So the key question isn't really "when will robots be perfect." It's "when will they be good enough that people want them around while they're still learning." Once you cross that line, the system gets more data, gets better, gets deployed more widely, and so on.

The other piece is that we're getting better at learning from experience itself, not just imitating demonstrations. That means reinforcement learning, learning from corrections, learning from autonomous practice. A robot that can take a task it does at 80% and get it to 95% or 99% through its own experience is a very different proposition from one that's frozen at whatever its training data gave it.

I'd compare it to the early days of self-driving, but with a better structure. With driving, you need near-perfect reliability before you can deploy at all, because mistakes are catastrophic. A lot of manipulation tasks are much more forgiving. If a robot drops a shirt while folding laundry, it picks it up and tries again. That tolerance for error is exactly what lets you start the flywheel early.

So I don't think we're waiting on some fundamental breakthrough. It's more a matter of scaling, engineering, and finding the right initial applications. That's why I think it's a matter of years rather than decades.

r001.rationale: The response says useful robot deployments in narrower settings could happen in one to two years, before a more general system, linking narrower scope to earlier deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's closer than most people assume, but not in the way they picture it. If you mean a general-purpose home robot that does your laundry and cooks dinner, that's still a ways off. But if you mean robots doing something economically useful in a narrow setting, learning from the experience they accumulate there, and then that experience making them better at the next thing—I think that starts within the next few years, and arguably it's already beginning.

The way I'd frame it is that the flywheel doesn't require the robot to be good at everything on day one. It requires the robot to be good enough at something that someone is willing to deploy it, and for the deployment to generate data that feeds back into training. That's the key shift from how robotics worked historically. Before, you'd engineer a system for a task, deploy it, and it would stay exactly as capable as the day you shipped it. With learning-based systems, every deployment is also a data collection run.

What's changed recently is that foundation models for robotics are starting to give you a reasonable prior. You're not starting from zero on each task anymore. So the question becomes: what's the first domain where the initial capability is just good enough? My guess is it's something fairly structured—logistics, some kinds of manufacturing, maybe certain commercial settings—where the environment has some regularity and the cost of a mistake is low. Not homes first. Homes are actually the hardest case because of the variability and the stakes.

The thing I'd caution against is the assumption that once the flywheel starts, it spins up instantly. There's a bootstrapping problem. Early on, the robot makes a lot of mistakes, and you need some combination of human oversight, teleoperation fallback, or clever reward design to turn those mistakes into useful signal rather than just failures. And you need the autonomy to be high enough that you're not just paying humans to babysit robots—at that point you don't have a flywheel, you have an expensive teleoperation business.

But I'm fairly optimistic. The pieces are there. We have models that can generalize across embodiments and tasks to a meaningful degree, we have a much better understanding of how to do reinforcement learning on real robots without breaking them, and there's actual commercial pressure to deploy. I'd say two to five years before you see the first real self-reinforcing loop in a deployed setting, and then the interesting question is how fast it compounds from there. That part I genuinely don't know—it could look like language models, where things accelerated faster than people expected, or it could be slower because the physical world imposes a data collection bottleneck that the internet never did.

r001.rationale: It contrasts general-purpose home robots, which are still a ways off, with robots deployed for economically useful tasks in narrow settings, which could begin within the next few years.

astra-6.text:
I think it could happen relatively soon, but I would distinguish between robots doing useful things in the real world and robots getting better automatically from that experience. Those are two different milestones.

You could deploy a robot that does a fairly narrow task, collect data when it fails, and then have engineers use that data to improve the system. That’s already a kind of flywheel. The more interesting version is where the robot can actually use its own experience to learn, and the amount of human effort required doesn’t grow proportionally with the number of robots.

The challenge is getting to a level of reliability where the robot is useful enough that somebody wants to deploy it, while still giving it opportunities to learn. If it needs a person standing next to it all the time, the economics are difficult. But if it can do most of the task and ask for help occasionally, then you have a plausible starting point: the help gets it unstuck, and it also provides information that could make it more autonomous next time.

So I’m cautiously optimistic about the next few years. I don’t think the first step has to be a robot that can do everything a person can do. It has to be something useful enough to keep operating, with a learning system that can turn that operation into improvement. Whether those improvements then generalize beyond the initial task is the really important question.

r001.rationale: The response presents a fairly narrow task as a plausible early deployment and says the first step need not be a robot that can do everything a person can do, communicating that limited scope enables earlier real-world use.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by real-world use. If we mean a robot that you can put in any home and ask it to do whatever you want, that’s a very high bar. If we mean robots doing a limited set of useful tasks in an environment where somebody can help them when they get stuck, I think that could happen much sooner.

The interesting threshold is when the robot is useful enough that someone wants to deploy it, but it still encounters things that it doesn’t know how to do. If those failures can become training data—perhaps with a person stepping in and showing it what to do—then deployment can improve the system, which makes further deployment more attractive.

But that flywheel isn’t automatic. Collecting experience is not the same as learning from it. You need a way to identify what went wrong, get useful supervision, and turn that into an improvement without breaking the things the robot could already do. I’m more uncertain about how quickly we’ll get that whole process working reliably than I am about whether we can produce impressive robot demonstrations.

So I would expect this to start in fairly constrained applications, with substantial human support, and broaden from there. You don’t need to solve all of robotics to get the process started. You need one application where the useful work the robot does justifies the cost of operating it and helping it learn.

r001.rationale: The candidate says robots handling a limited set of useful tasks could enter real-world use much sooner, and expects deployment to begin in constrained applications.
